entries.65c1c6a34a1018945bbc09a42905e4d0aed16e93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4730"/><div sID="gen6868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4730"/>23. The catalogue of my sins ought to be great, to judge from the severity with which God ever anew crushes one already bowed down. Would that He would reckon them up! He then would see how much my calamities outnumber them.<div eID="gen6868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin?--</hi>singular, "I am unconscious of a single particular sin, much less many" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6869" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b554cbe7222b3a6b704be60f12e2302b26f0dc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4731"/><div sID="gen6870" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4731"/><hi type="bold">24. hidest ... face--</hi>a figure from the gloomy impression caused by the sudden clouding over of the sun.<div eID="gen6870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enemy--</hi>God treated Job as an enemy who must be robbed of power by ceaseless sufferings (<reference osisRef="Job.7.17">Job 7:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.21">21</reference>). <div eID="gen6871" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f866371adebfd02ff614c727ba6157873254e38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4732"/><div sID="gen6872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4732"/>25. (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Le 26:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>). Job compares himself to a leaf already fallen, which the storm still chases hither and thither.<div eID="gen6872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break--</hi>literally, "shake with (Thy) terrors." Jesus Christ does not "break the bruised reed" (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.3">Is 42:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">27:8</reference>). <div eID="gen6873" type="x-p"/>
entries.321247ff8c8e35451a3cf44fd4c46b9e2df4b4fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4733"/><div sID="gen6874" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4733"/><hi type="bold">26. writest--</hi>a judicial phrase, to note down the determined punishment. The sentence of the condemned used to be written down (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.1">Is 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.30">Jr 22:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.149.9">Psa 149:9</reference>) [Umbreit].<div eID="gen6874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bitter things--</hi>bitter punishments.<div eID="gen6875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">makest me to possess--</hi>or "inherit." In old age he receives possession of the inheritance of sin thoughtlessly acquired in youth. "To inherit sins" is to inherit the punishments inseparably connected with them in Hebrew ideas (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">Psa 25:7</reference>). <div eID="gen6876" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e8fbd0946897c5280f7068778c40de3bdd24fea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4734"/><div sID="gen6877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4734"/><hi type="bold">27. stocks--</hi>in which the prisoner's feet were made fast until the time of execution (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.2">Jr 20:2</reference>).<div eID="gen6877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lookest narrowly--</hi>as an overseer would watch a prisoner.<div eID="gen6878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">print--</hi>Either the stocks, or his disease, marked his soles (Hebrew, "roots") as the bastinado would. Better, thou drawest (or diggest) [Gesenius] a line (or trench) [Gesenius] round my soles, beyond which I must not move [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6879" type="x-p"/>
entries.113b78873840ab017cf4ee2ab8530c8141b58262: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4735"/><div sID="gen6880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4735"/>28. Job speaks of himself in the third person, thus forming the transition to the general lot of man (<reference osisRef="Job.14.1">Job 14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.12">Ho 5:12</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.13"/>

entries.5eccea46bb5c32ebaa310eff731cb478944fdd96: <div eID="gen16408" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16409" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16410" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16410" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16409" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16411" type="x-p"/> Job defends himself against the accusations of his friends, and accuses them of endeavoring to pervert truth, <reference osisRef="Job.13.1-Job.13.8">Job 13:1-8</reference>. Threatens them with God's judgments, <reference osisRef="Job.13.9-Job.13.12">Job 13:9-12</reference>. Begs some respite, and expresses strong confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Job.13.13-Job.13.19">Job 13:13-19</reference>. He pleads with God, and deplores his severe trials and sufferings, <reference osisRef="Job.13.20-Job.13.28">Job 13:20-28</reference>. <div eID="gen16411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16412" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16413" type="x-p"/> Lo, mine eye hath seen all this - Ye have brought nothing new to me; I know those maxims as well as you: nor have you any knowledge of which I am not possessed.
entries.16ee68eff0d1229fd7e80230308b7307e85d46cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16414" type="x-p"/> Surely I would speak to the Almighty - אולם ulam, O that: - I wish I could speak to the Almighty! <div eID="gen16414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16415" type="x-p"/> I desire to reason with God - He speaks here to reference to the proceedings in a court of justice. Ye pretend to be advocates for God, but ye are forgers of lies: O that God himself would appear! Before him I could soon prove my innocence of the evils with which ye charge me.
entries.711a36f90c4d147492386a2be90b1e45b1557ffb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16416" type="x-p"/> Ye are forgers of lies - Ye frame deceitful arguments: ye reason sophistically, and pervert truth and justice, in order to support your cause. <div eID="gen16416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16417" type="x-p"/> Physicians of no value - Ye are as feeble in your reasonings as ye are inefficient in your skill. Ye can neither heal the wound of my mind, nor the disease of my body. In ancient times every wise man professed skill in the healing art, and probably Job's friends had tried their skill on his body as well as on his mind. He therefore had, in his argument against their teaching, a double advantage: Your skill in divinity and physic is equal: in the former ye are forgers of lies; in the latter, ye are good-for-nothing physicians. I can see no reason to depart from the general meaning of the original to which the ancient versions adhere. The Chaldee says: "Ye are idle physicians; and, like the mortified flesh which is cut off with the knife, so are the whole of you." The imagery in the former clause is chirurpical, and refers to the sewing together, or connecting the divided sides of wounds; for טפלי topheley, which we translate forgers, comes from טפל taphal, to fasten, tie, connect, sew together. And I question whether טפלי topheley here may not as well express Surgeons, as רפאי ropheey, in the latter clause, Physicians. Ye are Chirurgeons of falsity, and worthless Physicians.
entries.45798fce027d95dc32a2f76d72726d80d2ed2683: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16418" type="x-p"/> Hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom - In <reference osisRef="Pro.17.28">Pro 17:28</reference> we have the following apophtheym: "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise; and he that shutteth his lips, a man of understanding." There is no reason to say that Solomon quotes from Job: I have already expressed my opinion that the high antiquity attributed to this book is perfectly unfounded, and that there is much more evidence that Solomon was its author, than there is that it was the composition of Moses. But, whenever Job lived, whether before Abraham or after Moses, the book was not written till the time of Solomon, if not later. But as to the saying in question, it is a general apophthegm, and may be found among the wise sayings of all nations. I may observe here, that a silent man is not likely to be a fool; for a fool will be always prating, or, according to another adage, a fool's bolt is soon shot. The Latins have the same proverb: Vir sapit, qui pauca loquitur, "A wise man speaks little."
entries.05b5c98287724439f0b4974f4f194373e6c4baa3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16419" type="x-p"/> Hear now my reasoning - The speeches in this book are conceived as it delivered in a court of justice, different counselors pleading against each other. Hence most of the terms are forensic.
entries.105bc13e53b81b1d6aba61245a6d21a007e7431c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16420" type="x-p"/> Will ye speak wickedly for God? - In order to support your own cause, in contradiction to the evidence which the whole of my life bears to the uprightness of my heart, will ye continue to assert that God could not thus afflict me, unless flagrant iniquity were found in my ways; for it is on this ground alone that ye pretend to vindicate the providence of God. Thus ye tell lies for God's sake, and thus ye wickedly contend for your Maker.
entries.48f25b53e05fd21fbfbeedd62d7e09715d650fc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16421" type="x-p"/> Will ye accept his person? - Do you think to act by him as you would by a mortal; and, by telling lies in his favor, attempt to conciliate his esteem?
entries.a6d20730d273f255372a2ca39ef59f88b94aacb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16422" type="x-p"/> Is it good that he should search you out? - Would it be to your credit if God should try your hearts, and uncover the motives of your conduct? Were you tried as I am, how would you appear? <div eID="gen16422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16423" type="x-p"/> Do ye so mock him? - Do ye think that you can deceive him; and by flattering speeches bring him to your terms, as you would bring an undiscerning, empty mortal, like yourselves?
entries.6ea90cec40982195fe9eb1047bf066eeda86ca12: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16424" type="x-p"/> He will surely reprove you - You may expect, not only his disapprobation, but his hot displeasure.
entries.91bb2ed43fffc5cd9f8827022d94bbaf668111c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16425" type="x-p"/> His dread fall upon you? - The very apprehension of his wrath is sufficient to crush you to nothing.
entries.5f70ad3522a727b394092628cb0c2a3ea89f030f: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16426" type="x-p"/> Your remembrances are like unto ashes - Your memorable sayings are proverbs of dust. This is properly the meaning of the original: זכרניכם משלי אפר zichroneycem mishley epher. This he speaks in reference to the ancient and reputedly wise sayings which they had so copiously quoted against him. <div eID="gen16426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16427" type="x-p"/> Your bodies to bodies of clay - This clause is variously translated: Your swelling heaps are swelling heaps of mire. That is, Your high-flown speeches are dark, involved, and incoherent; they are all sound, no sense; great swelling words, either of difficult or no meaning, or of no point as applicable to my case.
entries.c21e8ac93d9ef81f810e6c4a2627d7312803b29b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16428" type="x-p"/> Hold your peace - You have perverted righteousness and truth, and your pleadings are totally irrelevant to the case; you have traveled out of the road; you have left law and justice behind you; it is high time that you should have done. <div eID="gen16428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16429" type="x-p"/> Let come on me what will - I will now defend myself against you, and leave the cause to its issue.
entries.5f246dcbd3434e5dd4792c990fa4e45e54894abc: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16430" type="x-p"/> Wherefore do I take my flesh in my teeth - A proverbial expression. I risk every thing on the justice of my cause. I put my life in my hand, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21">1Sam 28:21</reference>. I run all hazards; I am fearless of the consequences.
entries.2ddbefa7d76e2ebb2fedb09afaf7e107ae66aaf9: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16431" type="x-p"/> Though he slay me - I have no dependence but God; I trust in him alone. Should he even destroy my life by this affliction, yet will I hope that when he has tried me, I shall come forth as gold. In the common printed Hebrew text we have לא איחל lo ayachel, I will Not hope; but the Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee have read לו lo, Him, instead of לא lo Not; with twenty-nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and the Complutensian and Antwerp Polyglots. Our translators have followed the best reading. Coverdale renders the verse thus: Lo, there is nether comforte ner hope for me, yf he wil slaye me. <div eID="gen16431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16432" type="x-p"/> But I will maintain mine own ways - I am so conscious of my innocence, that I fear not to defend myself from your aspersions, even in the presence of my Maker.
entries.835bdc4f287542f7429ebd3fc05d8937c7e31e90: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16433" type="x-p"/> He also shall be my salvation - He will save me, because I trust in him. <div eID="gen16433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16434" type="x-p"/> A hypocrite - A wicked man shall never be able to stand before him. I am conscious of this, and were I, as you suppose, a secret sinner, I should not dare to make this appeal.
entries.adbadd357097be8ccefb788112fb99936386658c: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16435" type="x-p"/> Behold now, I have ordered - I am now ready to come into court, and care not how many I have to contend with, provided they speak truth.
entries.04155a67c8a35807c292b37ce8bc9c658063f879: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16436" type="x-p"/> Who is he that will plead with me? - Let my accuser, the plaintiff, come forward; I will defend my cause against him. <div eID="gen16436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16437" type="x-p"/> I shall give up the ghost - I shall cease to breathe. Defending myself will be as respiration unto me; or, While he is stating his case, I will be so silent as scarcely to appear to breathe.
entries.90288753f3c18238c628adbf769715133c29c37e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16438" type="x-p"/> Only do not two things unto me - These two things are the following: <div eID="gen16438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16439" type="x-p"/> 1. Withdraw thine hand far from me - remove the heavy affliction which thy hand has inflicted. <div eID="gen16439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16440" type="x-p"/> 2. Let not thy dread make me afraid - terrify me not with dreadful displays of thy majesty. The reasons of this request are sufficiently evident: <div eID="gen16440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16441" type="x-p"/> 1. How can a man stand in a court of justice and plead for his life, when under grievous bodily affliction? Withdraw thy hand far from me. <div eID="gen16441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16442" type="x-p"/> 2. Is it to be expected that a man can be sufficiently recollected, and in self-possession, to plead for his life, when he is overwhelmed with the awful appearance of the judge, the splendor of the court, and the various ensigns of justice? Let not thy dread make me afraid.
entries.e1a12cb3f129dc66cbee28366e6a2f19396788f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16443" type="x-p"/> Then call thou - Begin thou first to plead, and I will answer for myself; or, I will first state and defend my own case, and then answer thou me.
entries.cde037c11dbd4db0bbadaff2323caf6f7e20b235: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16444" type="x-p"/> How many are mine iniquities - Job being permitted to begin first, enters immediately upon the subject; and as it was a fact that he was grievously afflicted, and this his friends asserted was in consequence of grievous iniquities, he first desires to have them specified. What are the specific charges in this indictment? To say I must be a sinner to be thus afflicted, is saying nothing; tell me what are the sins, and show me the proofs.
entries.89d3f2344acad13ffd6571e97f923334f84558b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16445" type="x-p"/> Wherefore hidest thou thy face - Why is it that I no longer enjoy thy approbation? <div eID="gen16445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16446" type="x-p"/> Holdest me for thine enemy? - Treatest me as if I were the vilest of sinners?
entries.2ff12834720220f12def0b7b6f1f46590c8ae4fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16447" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou break a leaf - Is it becoming thy dignity to concern thyself with a creature so contemptible?
entries.d13b9208e039af4778974022c45c0e8ce20bf074: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16448" type="x-p"/> Thou writest bitter things against me - The indictment is filled with bitter or grievous charges, which, if proved, would bring me to bitter punishment. <div eID="gen16448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16449" type="x-p"/> The iniquities of my youth - The Levities and indiscretions of my youth I acknowledge; but is this a ground on which to form charges against a man the integrity of whose life is unimpeachable?
entries.5fa3b31f69970646f53030ec74963556a74a7d88: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16450" type="x-p"/> Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks - בסד bassad, "in a clog," such as was tied to the feet of slaves, to prevent them from running away. This is still used in the West Indies, among slave-dealers; and is there called the pudding, being a large collar of iron, locked round the ankle of the unfortunate man. Some have had them twenty pounds' weight; and, having been condemned to carry them for several years, when released could not walk without them! A case of this kind I knew: The slave had learned to walk well with his pudding, but when taken off, if he attempted to walk, he fell down, and was obliged to resume it occasionally, till practice had taught him the proper center of gravity, which had been so materially altered by wearing so large a weight; the badge at once of his oppression, and of the cruelty of his task-masters! <div eID="gen16450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16451" type="x-p"/> And lookest narrowly - Thou hast seen all my goings out and comings in; and there is no step I have taken in life with which thou art unacquainted. <div eID="gen16451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16452" type="x-p"/> Thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet - Some understand this as the mark left on the foot by the clog; or the owner's mark indented on this clog; or, Thou hast pursued me as a hound does his game, by the scent.
entries.87a1aafc0bb5c819382f890724e289f8f36c865e: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16453" type="x-p"/> And he, as a rotten thing - I am like a vessel made of skin; rotten, because of old age, or like a garment corroded by the moth. So the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic understood it. The word he may refer to himself.  <chapter eID="Job.13"/> <div eID="gen16453" type="x-p"/>

entries.ca7b73cf0fafb93c2ec9b678612ec589c11f8f8e: <reference osisRef="Job.13.1-Job.2.1">Job 13:1-2   1</reference>  Lo, mine eye hath seen all, <div eID="gen7348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7349" type="x-p"/> Mine ear hath heard and marked it.   2  What ye know do I know also, <div eID="gen7349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7350" type="x-p"/> I do not stand back behind you. <div eID="gen7350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7351" type="x-p"/> Job has brought forward proof of what he has stated at the commencement of this speech (<reference osisRef="Job.12.3">Job 12:3</reference>), that he is not inferior to them in the knowledge of God and divine things, and therefore he can now repeat as proved what he maintains. The plain כּל, which in other passages, with the force of הכּל, signifies <hi type="italic">omnes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen 16:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.5">Isa 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.12">Jer 44:12</reference>) and <hi type="italic">omnia</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.42.2">Job 42:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.7">Psa 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference>), has the definite sense of <hi type="italic">haec omnia</hi> here. לה (v. 1 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) is not after the Aramaic manner <hi type="italic">dat. pro acc. objecti:</hi> my ear has heard and comprehended it (<hi type="italic">id</hi>); but <hi type="italic">dat. commodi,</hi> or perhaps only <hi type="italic">dat. ethicus:</hi> and has made it intelligible to itself (<hi type="italic">sibi</hi>); בּין of the apprehension accompanying perception. He has a knowledge of the exalted and glorious majesty of God, acquired partly from his own observation and partly from the teachings of others. He also knows equal to (<hi type="italic">instar</hi>) their knowledge, i.e., he has a knowledge (ידע as the idea implied in it, e.g., like <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference>) which will bear comparison with theirs. But he will no longer contend with them.
entries.7cad303772fd8b2bfb19755252dd94ef50fd52f4: <reference osisRef="Job.13.3-Job.6.3">Job 13:3-6   3</reference>  But I would speak to the Almighty, <div eID="gen7351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7352" type="x-p"/> And I long to reason with God.   4  And ye however are forgers of lies, <div eID="gen7352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7353" type="x-p"/> Physicians of no value are ye all.   5  Oh that ye would altogether hold your peace, <div eID="gen7353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7354" type="x-p"/> It would be accounted to you as wisdom.   6  Hear now my instruction, <div eID="gen7354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7355" type="x-p"/> Ando hearken to the answers of my lips! <div eID="gen7355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7356" type="x-p"/> He will no longer dispute with the friends; the more they oppose him, the more earnestly he desires to be able to argue his cause before God. אוּלם (<reference osisRef="Job.13.3">Job 13:3</reference>) is disjunctive, like ἀλλά, and introduces a new range of thoughts; lxx ου ̓ μήν δὲ ἀλλά, <hi type="italic">verum enim vero. </hi> True, he has said in Job 9 that no one can maintain his cause before God; but his confidence in God grows in proportion as his distrust of the friends increases; and at the same time, the hope is begotten that God will grant him that softening of the terror of His majesty which he has reserved to himself in connection with this declaration (<reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference>, comp. Job 13:20.). The <hi type="italic">infin. absol.</hi> הוכח, which in <reference osisRef="Job.6.25">Job 6:25</reference> is used almost as a substantive, and indeed as the subject, is here in the place of the object, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference> : to prove, i.e., my cause, to God (אל־אל, like <reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>, אל־פּניו) I long. With ואוּלם (<reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>) the antithesis is introduced anew: I will turn to God, you on the contrary (καὶ ὑμεῖς δὲ). Since the verb טפל, from its primary meaning to spread on, smear on (whence e.g., Talmudic טפלה, the act of throwing on, as when plastering up the cracks of an oven), cogn. תּפל (whence תּפל, plaster, and perhaps also in the signification tasteless, <reference osisRef="Job.6.6">Job 6:6</reference> = sticky, greasy, slimy), does not signify, at least not at first, <hi type="italic">consuere</hi>, but <hi type="italic">assuere</hi> (without any relation of root with תּפר), we explain, not with Olshausen and others, <hi type="italic">concinnatores mendacii,</hi> such as sew together lies as patchwork; but with Hirzel and others, <hi type="italic">assutores mendacii,</hi> such as patch on lies, i.e., charge falsely, since they desire throughout to make him out to be a sinner punished according to his desert. This explanation is also confirmed by Job 14:17. Another explanation is given by Hupfeld: <hi type="italic">sarcinatores false </hi>= <hi type="italic">inanes, inutiles</hi>, so that שׁקר signifies what lies = what deceives, as in the parallel member of the verse אלל,<note placement="foot">In the Talmudic, the jugular vein, the cutting of which produces death, is called אלל (later עצב, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ṣb</hi>), according to which (<hi type="italic">b. Chullin</hi> 121a) it is explained: healer of the jugular artery, i.e., those who try to heal what is incurable, therefore charlatans, - a strange idea, which has arisen from the defective form of writing אלל. The lxx translates ἰαταὶ κακῶν.</note> nothingness, and also עמל (<reference osisRef="Job.16.2">Job 16:2</reference>) in a similar connection, is not an objective but attributive genitive; but <reference osisRef="Ps.119.69">Psa 119:69</reference> is decisive against this interpretation of שׁקר טפלי. The parallelism is not so exactly adjusted, as e.g., even רפאי does not on account of the parallel with טפלי signify patchers, ῥάπται, but: they are not able to heal Job’s wounds with the medicine of consolation; they are <hi type="italic">medici nihili</hi>, useless physicians. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.28">Pro 17:28</reference>, “Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise,” applies to them, <hi type="italic">si tacuisses, sapiens mansisses;</hi> or, as a rabbinical proverb of similar meaning, quoted by Heidenheim, says, השׂגה בהשׂגה הלאות, “the fatigue of comprehension is comprehension,” i.e., the silent pause before a problem is half the solution. The jussive form וּתהי, it would be (Ges. §128, 2), is used in the conclusion of the wish. Thus he challenges them to hear his תּוכחת (תּוכחה) and his רבוה. Hirzel is quite right when he says the former does not mean defence (justification), nor the latter proofs (counter-evidence); תוכחת is, according to his signification (<hi type="italic">significatus</hi>, in distinction from sensus), ἔλεγχος, <hi type="italic">correptio</hi> (lxx, Vulg.), and here not so much refutation and answer, as correction in an ethical sense, in correspondence with which רבות is also intended of reproaches, reproofs, or reprimands.
entries.9f3689932d7cadef4b03d18483987190622cebf3: <reference osisRef="Job.13.7-Job.11.7">Job 13:7-11   7</reference>  Will ye speak what is wrong for God, <div eID="gen7356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7357" type="x-p"/> And speak what is deceitful for Him?   8  Will ye be partial for Him, <div eID="gen7357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7358" type="x-p"/> Or will ye play the part of God’s advocates?   9  Would it be pleasant if He should search you out, <div eID="gen7358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7359" type="x-p"/> Or can ye jest with Him, as one jesteth with men? 10  He will surely expose you <div eID="gen7359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7360" type="x-p"/> If ye secretly act with partiality. 11  Will not His majesty confound you, <div eID="gen7360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7361" type="x-p"/> And His fear fall upon you? <div eID="gen7361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7362" type="x-p"/> Their advocacy of God - this is the thought of this strophe - is an injustice to Job, and an evil service rendered to God, which cannot escape undisguised punishment from Him. They set themselves up as God’s advocates (לאל ריב, like לבּעל ריב, Jdg 6:31), and at the same time accept His person, <hi type="italic">accipiunt</hi> (as in <hi type="italic">acceptus</hi> = <hi type="italic">gratus</hi>), or lift it up, i.e., favour, or give preference to, His person, viz., at the expense of the truth: they are partial in His favour, as they are twice reminded and given to understand by the <hi type="italic">fut. energicum</hi> תּשּׂאוּן. The addition of בּסּתר (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.10">Job 13:10</reference></hi>) implies that they conceal their better knowledge by the assumption of an earnest tone and bearing, expressive of the strongest conviction that they are in the right. They know that Job is not a flagrant sinner; nevertheless they deceive themselves with the idea that he is, and by reason of this delusion they take up the cause of God against him. Such perversion of the truth <hi type="italic">in majorem Dei gloriam</hi> is an abomination to God. When He searches them, His advocates, out (חקר, as Prov.Job 28:11), they will become conscious of it; or will God be mocked, as one mocketh mortal men? Comp. <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Gal 6:7</reference> for a similar thought. חתל is <hi type="italic">inf. absol. </hi>after the form תּללּ, and תּהתלּוּ is also to be derived from תּללּ, and is <hi type="italic">fut. Hiph.,</hi> the preformative not being syncopated, for תּתלּוּ (Ges. §53, rem. 7); not <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, from התל (as 1Ki 18:27), with the doubling of the middle radical resolved (Olsh. in his <hi type="italic">Lehrb</hi>. S. 577). God is not pleased with λατρεία (Joh 16:2) which gives the honour to Him, but not to truth, such ζῆλος Θεοῦ ἀλλ ̓ ου ̓ κατ ̓ ἐπίγνωσιν (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Rom 10:2</reference>), such advocacy contrary to one’s better knowledge and conscience, in which the end is thought to sanctify the means. Such advocacy must be put to shame and confounded when He who needs no concealment of the truth for His justification is manifest in His שׂאת, i.e., not: in the kindling of His wrath (after Jdg 20:38; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>), but: in His exaltation (correctly by Ralbag: התנשׂאותו ורוממותו), and by His direct influence brings all untruth to light. It is the boldest thought imaginable, that one dare not have respect even to the person of God when one is obliged to lie to one’s self. And still it is also self-evident. For God and truth can never be antagonistic.
entries.7e4c44f9873a28d39377f76557a013fc5692e679: Job 13:12-16 12  Your memorable words are proverbs of dust, <div eID="gen7362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7363" type="x-p"/> Your strongholds are become strongholds of clay! 13  Leave me in peace, and I will speak, <div eID="gen7363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7364" type="x-p"/> And let what will come on me. 14  Wherefore should I bear my flesh in my teeth? <div eID="gen7364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7365" type="x-p"/> I take my soul in my hands. 15  Behold, He slayeth me-I wait for Him: <div eID="gen7365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7366" type="x-p"/> I will only prove my way before Him. 16  Even this would by my salvation, <div eID="gen7366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7367" type="x-p"/> That a hypocrite dare not appear before Him. <div eID="gen7367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7368" type="x-p"/> The words by which they exhort and warn him are called זכרנים, not because they recall the experience and teaching of the ancients (Hirz.), but as sayings to which attention and thought should be given, with the tone of זכר־נא, <reference osisRef="Job.4.7">Job 4:7</reference> (Hahn); as ספר זכרון, Mal 3:16, the book of remembrance; and ספר זכרנות, <reference osisRef="Esth.6.1">Est 6:1</reference>, the book of memorabilia or memoranda. These their <hi type="italic">loci communes</hi> are proverbs of ashes, i.e., proverbs which in respect to the present case, say nothing, passing away like ashes (אפר = vanity, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.20">Isa 44:20</reference>). While <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.12">Job 13:12</reference></hi> says what their speeches, with the weighty <hi type="italic">nota bene,</hi> are, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.12">Job 13:12</reference></hi> says what their גּבּים become; for ל always denotes a κίνησις = γένεσις, and is never the exponent of the predicate in a simple clause.<note placement="foot">The Jewish expositors compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.2">1Ch 3:2</reference> on לגבי, but the ל there in לאבשׁלום is a clerical error (comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.3">2Sa 3:3</reference>). Reiske conjectures רגבי (lumps of clay), one of the best among his most venturesome conjectures.</note> <div eID="gen7368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7369" type="x-p"/> Like the Arabic <hi type="italic">dahr</hi>, גּב signifies a boss, back, then protection, bulwark, rampart: their arguments or proofs are called גבים (עצּמות, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.21">Isa 41:21</reference>; comp. ὀχυρώματα, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>); these ramparts which they throw up become as ramparts of clay, will be shown to be such by their being soon broken through and falling in. Their reasons will not stand before God, but, like clay that will not hold together, fall to pieces.
entries.248b96162a6ca4d5b36d19914f3b8c9764837be5: Job 13:17-19 17  Hear, O hear my confession, <div eID="gen7376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7377" type="x-p"/> And let my declaration echo in your ears. 18  Behold now! I have arranged the cause, <div eID="gen7377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7378" type="x-p"/> I know that I shall maintain the right. 19  Who then can contend with me? <div eID="gen7378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7379" type="x-p"/> Then, indeed, I would be silent and expire. <div eID="gen7379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7380" type="x-p"/> Eager for the accomplishment of his wish that he might himself take his cause before God, and as though in imagination it were so, he invites the friends to be present to hear his defence of himself. מלּה (in Arabic directly used for confession = religion) is the confession which he will lay down, and אחוה the declaration that he will make in evidence, i.e., the proof of his innocence. The latter substantive, which signifies brotherly conduct in post-biblical Hebrew, is here an ἅπ. λεγ. from חוה, not however with <hi type="italic">Aleph prostheticum</hi> from <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, but after the form אזכּרה = הזכּרה, from the <hi type="italic">Aphêl</hi> = <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> of this verb, which, except <reference osisRef="Ps.19.3">Psa 19:3</reference>, occurs only in the book of Job as Hebrew (comp. the <hi type="italic">n. actionis,</hi> אחויה, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.12">Dan 5:12</reference>), Ewald, §156, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. It is unnecessary to carry the שׁמעוּ on to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.17">Job 13:17</reference></hi> (hear now ... with your own ears, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">Jer 26:11</reference>); <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.17">Job 13:17</reference></hi> is an independent substantival clause like <reference osisRef="Job.15.11">Job 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Isa 5:9</reference>, which carries in itself the verbal idea of תּהי or תּבא (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>). They shall hear, for on his part he has arranged, i.e., prepared (משׁפּט ערך, <hi type="italic">causam instruere,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.23.4">Job 23:4</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.33.5">Job 33:5</reference>) the cause, so that the action can begin forthwith; and he knows that he, he and no one else, will be found in the right. With the conviction of this superiority, he exclaims, Who in all the world could contend with him, i.e., advance valid arguments against his defence of himself? Then, indeed, if this impossibility should happen, he would be dumb, and willingly die as one completely overpowered not merely in outward appearance, but in reality vanquished. יריב עמדי following הוא מי (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.4.7">Job 4:7</reference>) may be taken as an elliptical relative clause: <hi type="italic">qui litigare possit mecum</hi> (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.50.9">Isa 50:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">Rom 8:34</reference>, τίς ὁ καταδρίνων); but since זה הוא מי is also used in the sense of <hi type="italic">quis tandem</hi> or <hi type="italic">ecquisnam</hi>, this syntactic connection which certainly did exist (Ewald, §325, <hi type="italic">a</hi>) is obliterated, and הוא serves like זה only to give intensity and vividness to the מי. On עתּה כּי (in meaning not different to אז כּי), vid., <reference osisRef="Job.3.13">Job 3:13</reference>; Job 8:6. In <reference osisRef="Job.13.19">Job 13:19</reference> that is granted as possible which, according to the declaration of his conscience, Job must consider as absolutely impossible. Therefore he clings to the desire of being able to bring his cause before God, and becomes more and more absorbed in the thought.
entries.2e0e1f3f7a73e0575ed20111ede4b3b868408ec1: Job 13:20-22 20  Only two things do not unto me, <div eID="gen7380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7381" type="x-p"/> Then will I not hide myself from Thy countenance: 21  Withdraw Thy hand from me, <div eID="gen7381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7382" type="x-p"/> And let Thy fear not terrify me - 22  Call then and I will answer, <div eID="gen7382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7383" type="x-p"/> Or I will speak and answer Thou me! <div eID="gen7383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7384" type="x-p"/> He makes only two conditions in his prayer, as he has already expressed it in <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference> : (<reference osisRef="Job.9.1">1</reference>) That God would grant him a cessation of his troubles; (2) That He would not overwhelm him with His majesty. The chastening hand of God is generally called יד elsewhere; but in spite of this prevalent usage of the language, כּף cannot be understood here (comp. on the contrary <reference osisRef="Job.33.7">Job 33:7</reference>) otherwise than of the hand (<reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference> : the rod) of God, which lies heavily on Job. The painful pressure of that hand would prevent the collecting and ordering of his thoughts required for meeting with God, and the אימה (Codd. defectively אמתך) of God would completely crush and confound him. But if God grants these two things: to remove His hand for a time, and not to turn the terrible side of His majesty to him, then he is ready whether God should himself open the cause or permit him to have the first word. Correctly Mercerus: <hi type="italic">optionem ei dat ut aut actoris aut rei personam deligat, sua fretus innocentia, sed interim sui oblitus et immodicus.</hi> In contrast with God he feels himself to be a poor worm, but his consciousness of innocence makes him a Titan. <div eID="gen7384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7385" type="x-p"/> He now says what he would ask God; or rather, he now asks Him, since he vividly pictures to himself the action with God which he desires. His imagination anticipates the reality of that which is longed for. Modern expositors begin a new division at Job 13:23. But Job’s speech does not yet take a new turn; it goes on further continually <hi type="italic">uno tenore</hi>.
entries.459c322114961409dbeeb1b993307ededce6793f: Job 13:23-25 23  How many are mine iniquities and sins? <div eID="gen7385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7386" type="x-p"/> Make me to know my transgression and sin! -  - 24  Wherefore dost Thou hide Thy face, <div eID="gen7386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7387" type="x-p"/> And regard me as Thine enemy? 25  Wilt Thou frighten away a leaf driven to and fro, <div eID="gen7387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7388" type="x-p"/> And pursue the dry stubble? <div eID="gen7388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7389" type="x-p"/> When עון and חטּאת, פּשׁע and חטּאת, are used in close connection, the latter, which describes sin as failing and error, signifies sins of weakness (infirmities, <hi type="italic">Schwachheitssünde</hi>); whereas עון (prop. distorting or bending) signifies misdeed, and פשׁע (prop. breaking loose, or away from, Arab. <hi type="italic">fsq</hi>) wickedness which designedly estranges itself from God and removes from favour, both therefore malignant sin (<hi type="italic">Bosheitssünde</hi>).<note placement="foot">Comp. the development of the idea of the synonyms for sin in von Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, i. 483ff., at the commencement of the fourth <hi type="italic">Lehrstück</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen7389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7390" type="x-p"/> The bold self-confidence which is expressed in the question and challenge of <reference osisRef="Job.13.23">Job 13:23</reference> is, in <reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference>, changed to grievous astonishment that God does not appear to him, and on the contrary continues to pursue him as an enemy without investigating his cause. Has the Almighty then pleasure in scaring away a leaf that is already blown to and fro? העלה, with <hi type="italic">He interrog.,</hi> like החכם, <reference osisRef="Job.15.2">Job 15:2</reference>, according to Ges. §100, 4. ערץ used as transitive here, like <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">Psa 10:18</reference>, to terrify, scare away affrighted. Does it give Him satisfaction to pursue dried-up stubble? By את (before an indeterminate noun, according to Ges. §117, 2) he points δεικτικῶς to himself: he, the powerless one, completely deprived of strength by sickness and pain, is as dried-up stubble; nevertheless God is after him, as though He would get rid of every trace of a dangerous enemy by summoning His utmost strength against him.
entries.75d9f817fe52b83ae9172a1972b2309ec1765f48: Job 13:26-28 26  For Thou decreest bitter things against me, <div eID="gen7390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7391" type="x-p"/> And causest me to possess the iniquities of my youth, 27  And puttest my feet in the stocks, <div eID="gen7391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7392" type="x-p"/> And observest all my ways. <div eID="gen7392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7393" type="x-p"/> Thou makest for thyself a circle round the soles of my feet, 28  Round one who moulders away as worm-eaten, <div eID="gen7393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> As a garment that the moth gnaweth. <div eID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7395" type="x-p"/> He is conscious of having often prayed: “Remember not the sins of my youth, and my transgressions: according to Thy mercy remember Thou me,” <reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">Psa 25:7</reference>; and still he can only regard his affliction as the inheritance (i.e., entailed upon him by sins not repented of) of the sins of his youth, since he has no sins of his mature years that would incur wrath, to reproach himself with. He does not know how to reconcile with the justice of God the fact that He again records against him sins, the forgiveness of which he implores soon after their commission, and decrees (כּתב, as <reference osisRef="Ps.149.9">Psa 149:9</reference>, and as used elsewhere in the book of Job with reference to the recording of judgment) for him on account of them such bitter punishment (מררות, <hi type="italic">amara</hi>, bitter calamities; comp. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">Deu 32:32</reference>, “bitter” grapes). And the two could not indeed be harmonized, if it really were thus. So long as a man remains an object of the divine mercy, his sins that have been once forgiven are no more the object of divine judgment. But Job can understand his affliction only as an additional punishment. The conflict of temptation through which he is passing has made God’s loving-kindness obscure to him. He appears to himself to be like a prisoner whose feet are forced into the holes of a סד, i.e., the block or log of wood in which the feet of a criminal are fastened, and which he must shuffle about with him when he moves; perhaps connected with Arab. <hi type="italic">sadda , occludere, opplere</hi> (<hi type="italic">foramen</hi>), elsewhere מהפּכת (from the forcible twisting or fastening), Chald. סדיא, סדנא, Syr. <hi type="italic">sado ,</hi> by which <reference osisRef="Acts.16.24">Act 16:24</reference>, ξύλον = ποδοκάκη, is rendered; Lat. <hi type="italic">cippus</hi> (which Ralbag compares), <hi type="italic">codex</hi> (in Plautus an instrument of punishment for slaves), or also <hi type="italic">nervus</hi>. The verb תּשׂם which belongs to it, and is found also in <reference osisRef="Job.33.11">Job 33:11</reference> in the same connection, is of the jussive form, but is neither jussive nor optative in meaning, as also the future with shortened vowel (e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.27.22">Job 27:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.19">Job 40:19</reference>) or apocopated (<reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>) is used elsewhere from the preference of poetry for a short pregnant form. He seems to himself like a criminal whose steps are closely watched (שׁמר, as <reference osisRef="Job.10.14">Job 10:14</reference>), in order that he may not have the undeserved enjoyment of freedom, and may not avoid the execution for which he is reserved by effecting an escape by flight. Instead of ארחתי, the reading adopted by Ben-Ascher, Ben-Naphtali writes ארחתי, with <hi type="italic">Cholem</hi> in the first syllable; both modes of punctuation change without any fixed law also in other respects in the inflexion of ארח, as of ארחה, a caravan, the construct is both ארחות, <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>, and ארחות. It is scarcely necessary to remark that the verbs in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference></hi> are addressed to God, and are not intended as the <hi type="italic">third pers. fem.</hi> in reference to the stocks (Ralbag). The roots of the feet are undoubtedly their undermost parts, therefore the soles. But what is the meaning of תּתחקּה? The Vulg., Syr., and Parchon explain: Thou fixest thine attention upon ... , but certainly according to mere conjecture; Ewald, by the help of the Arabic <hi type="italic">tahhakkaka ala</hi>: Thou securest thyself ... , but there is not the least necessity to depart from the ordinary use of the word, as those also do who explain: Thou makest a law or boundary (Aben-Ezra, Ges., Hahn, Schlottm.). The verb חקה is the usual word (certainly cognate and interchangeable with חקק) for carved-out work (intaglio), and perhaps with colour rubbed in, or filled up with metal (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.14">Eze 23:14</reference>); it signifies to hew into, to carve, to dig a trench. Stickel is in some measure true to this meaning when he explains: Thou scratchest, pressest (producing blood); by which rendering, however, the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. is not duly recognised. Raschi is better, <hi type="italic">tu t'affiches</hi>, according to which Mercerus: <hi type="italic">velut affixus vestigiis pedum meorum adhaeres, ne quâ elabi possim aut effugere. </hi> But a closer connection with the ordinary use of the word is possible. Accordingly Rosenm., Umbreit, and others render: Thou markest a line round my feet (drawest a circle round); Hirz., however, in the strictest sense of the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>.: Thou diggest thyself in (layest thyself as a circular line about my feet). But the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. does not necessarily mean <hi type="italic">se insculpere</hi>, but, as התפשׁט <hi type="italic">sibi exuere,</hi> התפתח <hi type="italic">sibi solvere,</hi> התחנן <hi type="italic">sibi propitium facere,</hi> it may also mean sibi insculpere, which does not give so strange a representation: Thou makest to thyself furrows (or also: lines) round the soles of my feet, so that they cannot move beyond the narrow boundaries marked out by thee. With והוּא, <reference osisRef="Job.13.28">Job 13:28</reference>, a circumstantial clause begins: While he whom Thou thus fastenest in as a criminal, etc. Observe the fine rhythmical accentuation <hi type="italic">achālo ‛asch</hi>. Since God whom he calls upon does not appear, Job’s defiance is changed to timidity. The elegiac tone, into which his bold tone has passed, is continued in Job 14.  <chapter eID="Job.13"/> <div eID="gen7395" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a5628eb4c82c19a1df62c819e4fbbb102a418ef:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="13" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. LO, mine Eye hath seen all <ns0:hi>this,</ns0:hi> mine Ear hath heard and understood it <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi> this which either you or I have discoursed concerning the infinite Power and Wisdom of God, I know, both by <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> it, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> by my own Observation and Experience, and by <ns0:hi>hearing</ns0:hi> it from my Ancestors; so that I did not need your tedious and impertinent dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courses concerning those matters.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:394" />2. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12 3.</ns0:note> What ye know, <ns0:hi>the same</ns0:hi> do I know also: I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> not inferiour unto you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 23. 3.</ns0:note> Surely I would speak to the Almighty <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">According to thy Wish, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 11. 5. I had rather debate the matter with God than with you. I am not afraid of presenting my Person and Cause before him, who is a Witness of my Integrity, and would not deal so unmercifully with me as you do.</ns0:note>, and I desire to reason with God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. But ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> forgers of Lies <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Authors of False Doctrine, to wit, that great afflictions are peculiar to Hypocrites and wicked Men.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6. 21. & 16. 2.</ns0:note> ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> all Physici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans of no value <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Unfaithful and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />skilful, prescribing bad Remedies, and misapplying good ones.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. O that ye would altogether hold your peace, and it should be your Wisdom <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For then your Ignorance and Folly had been concealed, which is now manifest. Compare <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 28.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Hear <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Attend to it, and consider it more seriously than you have done.</ns0:note> now my reasoning, and hearken to the pleadings of my Lips <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To the arguments which I shall produce.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>p. 17. 5. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 32. 21. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 35. 4.</ns0:note> Will ye speak wickedly for God <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Will you utter falshoods upon pretence of pleasing God, or of maintaining Gods Honour or Justice? Doth he need such de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fences?</ns0:note>? And talk deceitfully for him?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Will ye accept his Person <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not judging according to the right of the Cause, but the qua<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lity of the Person, as corrupt Judges do.</ns0:note>? Will ye contend <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Wrangle and quarrel with me, and cavil at my Speeches, and pervert my meaning.</ns0:note> for God <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That you may gratifie him, or defend his Rights?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Is it good <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Will it be to your Credit and Comfort?</ns0:note> that he should search you out <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Narrowly ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />amine your Hearts and discourses, whether you have uttered Truth or Falshood; and whether your Speeches proceed from true Zeal for God, or from your own Prejudices and Passions, and from a desire to curry Favour with him.</ns0:note>? or as one mocketh another, do ye <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> mock him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To wit, by covering your un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />charitableness and corrupt affections with pretences of Piet<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, as if God could not discern your Artifices; or by pleading his Cause with weak and foolish Arguments, which is a kind of Mockery to him, and an Injury to his Cause; or by seeking to flatter him with false Praises, as if he did distribute the things of this world with exact Justice, prospering only the good, and severely af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flicting none but wicked Men.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. He will surely reprove you <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Punish you; as this word is o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t used, as hath been once and again observed.</ns0:note>, if ye do secretly <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Though it be concealed in your own Breasts, and no Eye see it; yea, though it be so close that your own Minds and Consciences, through ignorance, or inadvertency, or sloth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness, do not perceive it, yet he, who is greater than your Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sciences, sees and knows it.</ns0:note> accept Persons.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. Shall not his Excellency <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">His infinite Wisdom which sees your secret Falshoods, and his Justice and Power, which can and will punish you for it.</ns0:note> make you afraid <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Of speaking rashly or falsly of his ways and Counsels.</ns0:note>? And his dread fall upon you?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. Your remembrances <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either 1. Actively, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> your Memorials, or your Discourses and Arguments by which you design to bring things to my remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brance. So he might possibly allude to that passage, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 4. 7 <ns0:hi>Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />member I pray thee,</ns0:hi> &c. That and all your other Memento's <ns0:hi>are like unto ashes, i. e.</ns0:hi> contemptible and unprofitable: Heb. <ns0:hi>are Parables,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Speeches of dust,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>ashes.</ns0:hi> Or 2. Passively, all that which is most excellent and memorable in you; your Wealth, and Dignity, and Wit, and Reputation, or whatsoever it is for which you expect or desire to be remembered, it is all but poor despicable dust and ashes: And therefore you have just reason to abhor your selves, and to dread the Divine Majesty, as I now advised you.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like unto ashes, your Bodies <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Though they be not full of sores and boils as mine is, yet they are but dust, and to dust they shall return as well as mine. Heb. <ns0:hi>Your backs,</ns0:hi> which, being the strongest part of the Body, is put for the whole Body. Or, <ns0:hi>Your Eminences,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Excellencies,</ns0:hi> as this word most pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly signifies, as Hebricians observe so it answers to their <ns0:hi>memo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>bles.</ns0:hi> All those things wherein you do, or think that you do ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cel others, are but like Eminencies, or Lumps, or Heaps of Clay, vain and useless things, if compared with the Excellencies of God. Or, <ns0:hi>Your heights, i. e.</ns0:hi> your losty Discourses are like Clay, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out solidity and strength.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like to Bodies of Clay.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> be silens from me.</ns0:note> Hold your peace <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Do not now interrupt me in my Discourse; which peradventure he observed by their gestures some of them were now attempting.</ns0:note>, let me alone that I may speak <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That I may freely utter my whole mind.</ns0:note>, and let come on me what <ns0:hi>will</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">For the event of my Discourse with God, wherewith you threaten me, I am willing to submit my self to him, to do with me as he pleaseth: For I know he will not judge so severely and partially of me, or my words, as you do, but will accept what is good, and pass by any circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stantial defects in my Person or Speech, as knowing that I speak from an upright Heart.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. Wherefore do I take my Flesh in my Teeth, and put my Life in mine hand? <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">According to this Translation the sense seems to be this, If you speak truth, and God punisheth none but wicked men, why doth he bring me (whom he Knows to be no Hypocrite, as you slaunder me) to that extremity of Pain and misery, that I am almost constrained to tear, and eat my own flesh (which is mentioned as the Character of men in great anguish, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 9. 20. & 49. 26.) and am ready to lay violent hands upon my self? Is it so great a crime to complain in this case, or at least to enquire into the cause of this unwonted severity: But this sense seems not well to suit ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther with the foregoing or following Verses, but to come in abrupt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly. Others therefore render the words thus, <ns0:hi>Why should I take my flesh in my Teeth,</ns0:hi> &c. And so this may be either 1. A Reason of his ardent desire of Liberty of Speech, because he could hold his Tongue no longer, but must needs tear himself to pieces, if he had not some vent for his grief. So this agrees well both with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. where he desired this freedom, and with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. where the same sense is expressed in plainer words. Or 2. An Antidote against despair. I perceive O my Friends by your Discourses, that you intend to drive me to utter Despair, if I do not turn to God in a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother manner than yet I have done. Which if it were true, I should certainly tear my flesh, and violently take away my own Life: But I see no reason why I should give way to any such de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spair or desperate Actions? And this also hath a good dependance upon the foregoing words, <ns0:hi>Let come on me what will.</ns0:hi> But I have no reason to fear such Consequences as you suggest, nor to despair of a merciful Audience and Relief from God; and a good con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nexion with those which follow, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15. where he declares his Hope and Confidence in God. The Phrase of having ones <ns0:hi>Life in his hand,</ns0:hi> notes a condition extremely dangerous, and almost desperate, as <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 12. 3. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 5. & 28. 21. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119. 109.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 23. 4. Prov. 14. 32.</ns0:note> Though he slay me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Though God should yet more and more encrease my torments, so that I could bear them no longer, but should perceive my self to be at the point of Death, and without all hopes of Recovery in this World.</ns0:note>, yet I will trust in him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>shall I not trust</ns0:hi> in him? Should I despair? No, I will not. I know he is a just, and a faithful, and merciful God, and he knows that mine Heart is upright before him, and that I am no Hypocrite.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Though I will trust in him, yet I will humbly expostulate the matter with him.</ns0:note> I will <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> prove, or argue.</ns0:note> maintain mine own ways <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>I will argue,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>prove,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monstrate my ways, i. e.</ns0:hi> I will make a full free Confession of the whole course of my Life, and I will boldly, though submissively, assert mine own Integrity, which he also will<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> I doubt not ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledge. And what I have done amiss I will as freely confess; and make Supplication to my judge for the pardon of it.</ns0:note> before him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Before his Tribunal: for I desire no other Judge but him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. He also <ns0:hi>shall be,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my Salvation <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">I rest assured that he will save me out of these miseries sooner or later, one way or other, if not with a temporal, yet with an eternal Salvation after Death<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of which he speaks, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19. 25, &c.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>but,</ns0:hi> as this particle commonly signifies, for this Clause is put by way of opposition to the former, and the sense is<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> But if I were an Hypocrite as you alledge, I durst not present my self before him to plead my Cause with him, as now I desire to do, nor could I hope for any Salvation from, or with, him in Heaven.</ns0:note> an Hypocrite shall not come before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Hear diligently my Speech <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This he desired before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. and now repeateth, either be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they manifested some neglect or dislike of his Speech, and some desire to interrupt him: Or, because he now comes more closely to his business, the foregoing Verses being mostly in way of Preface to it.</ns0:note>, and my declara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The words whereby I declare my Mind.</ns0:note> with your Ears.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. Behold now, I have ordered <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Cause <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To wit, within my self. I have seriously and sincerely consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dered the state of my case, and what can be said either for me, or against me, and am ready to plead my Cause.</ns0:note>; I know that I shall be justified <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Acquitted by God from that Hypocrisie and Wickedness wherewith you charge me, and declared a righteous and innocent person, humane Infir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mities excepted.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:395" />19. Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> will plead with me <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Where is the man that will do it? Nay, Oh that God would do it: which here he implies, and presently expresseth.</ns0:note>? For now if I hold my Tongue, I shall give up the Ghost <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">My grief for Gods heavy Hand, and for your bitter Reproaches would break my Heart, if I should not give it vent.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. Only do not Two <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> unto me <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which Two he expresseth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21.</ns0:note>: then will I not hide my self from thee <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Then shall I boldly pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent my self and Cause before thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 9. 34, 35. & 33. 7.</ns0:note> Withdraw thine hand far from me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Suspend my Torments during the time of my pleading with thee, that my Mind may be at liberty.</ns0:note>: and let not thy dread make me afraid <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Do not present thy self to me in terrible Majest, neither deal with me in rigorous Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stice; but hear me meekly, as one man heareth another, and plead with me upon those gracious Terms, wherewith thou usest to deal with Mankind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. Then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Then chuse thy own Method. Either do thou charge me with Hypocrisie, or more than common Guilt, and I will de<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>end my self: Or I will argue with thee concerning thy extraordinary seve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity towards me; and do thou <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>hew me the reasons of it. This proposal savoured of too great self-confidence, and of Irreverence towards God; for which, and such like Speeches, he is reproved by God, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 38. 2, 3. & 40. 2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. How many <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> mine Iniquities and sins <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That I am a sinner I confess; but that I am guilty of so many or such heinous Crimes as my Friends suppose, I utterly deny; and if I be so, do thou, O Lord, discover it to my shame.</ns0:note>? Make me to know my transgression and my Sin <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">If peradventure my heart deceive me therein; for I am not consci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous to my self of any enormous crime.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. Wherefore hidest thou thy Face <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Withdrawest thy favour and help which thou didst use to afford me; as this Phrase is commonly used, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 31. 17. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 13. 1. & 102. 2. &c.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 32. 20. Ruth. 1, 21. Ch. 16. 9. & 19. 11. & 33. 10.</ns0:note> hold<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>st me for thine Enemy <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Dealest as harshly with me, as if I were thy professed Enemy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 42. 3.</ns0:note> Wilt thou break a Leaf driven to and fro? And wilt thou pursue the dry stubble <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Doth it become thy infinite and excellent Majesty to use all thy might to crush such a poor, impotent, frail Creature as I am, that can no more resist thy Power, than a Leaf, or a little loose and dry straw can resist the fury of the Wind or Fire.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. For thou writest <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou appointest or inflictest. A Metaphor from Princes or Judges, who antiently used to write their Sentences or Decrees, concerning Persons, or Causes, brought before them. See <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 149. 9. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 22. 30. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 19. 22.</ns0:note> bitter things <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A terrible Sentence, or most grievous punishments.</ns0:note> against me, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 25. 7.</ns0:note> makest me to possess the Iniquities of my Youth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Thou dost now at once bring upon me the punishment of all my sins, not excepting those of my Youth, which, because of the Folly and weakness of that Age, are usually excused or winked at, or, at least, but gently punished.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 11.</ns0:note> Thou puttest my Feet also in the stocks <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thou encompassest me with thy Judgments, that I may have no way or possibility to escape.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> observ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est.</ns0:note> lookest narrowly unto all my Paths <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">When thou hast me fast in Pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, thou makest a strict and diligent search into all the actions of my life, that thou m<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ist find matter to condemn me.</ns0:note>; thou settest a Print upon the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> roots.</ns0:note> Heels of my Feet <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou followest me close at the Heels, either to observe my Actions, or to pursue me with thy Judgments, so that thou dost oft tread upon my Heels, and leave the prints of thy Footsteps upon them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. And he <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either 1. Man, or <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> supposed to be Gods Adversary in this contest. So he speaks of himself in the third Person, as is usual in this and other sacred Books. So the Sense is, <ns0:hi>He, i. e.</ns0:hi> this poor frail Creature, this Carkass or Body of mine; which possibly he pointed a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> with his Finger, <ns0:hi>consumeth</ns0:hi> or pineth away, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> So he mentions here the effect of Gods severe proceedings against him, to wit, his Consum<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>tion, and utter Destruction, which was making haste towards him. Or, 2<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> God, of whom he hitherto spoke in the second Person, and now in the third Person, such changes of persons being very frequent in poetical Writings, such as this is. So he continueth the former Discourse, and as before he mentioned Gods severe Enquiry into his ways, and Sentence against him, so here he describes the Consequence and dreadful Execution of it upon him: <ns0:hi>He i. e.</ns0:hi> God, <ns0:hi>consumeth</ns0:hi> (for the Verb is Active) me <ns0:hi>as rottenness</ns0:hi> consumeth that in which it is, or <ns0:hi>as a rotten thing</ns0:hi> is consu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med, and <ns0:hi>as a Moth which eateth a Garment.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, as a rotten thing, consumeth as a Garment that is Moth-eaten.</ns0:p>
